input:
When a pure liquid is heated to its boiling point, something quite interesting happens: the liquid and its vapour are able to coexist in a state of phase equilibrium. Essentially, the underlying condition can be stated in words before any equation is introduced, namely that the chemical potential of the liquid phase is exactly equal to the chemical potential of the vapour phase. Chemical potential can be thought of as the driving force for material transfer, so whenever the two values are not equal, material moves from the phase with the higher value to the lower one, until equality is restored.

At the boiling point itself, the liquid and the vapour sit at the same temperature and the same pressure, and neither phase grows at the expense of the other. Interestingly, adding more heat at this stage does not make the temperature go up any further. Instead, the additional heat is consumed by the change of state itself, steadily converting liquid into vapour while the equality of the chemical potentials is preserved, since a rise in temperature would disturb the balance on which the coexistence depends.

It is important to note that the boiling point is not simply a fixed property of the liquid on its own. If the pressure is changed, the temperature at which the two chemical potentials become equal shifts as well, and boiling takes place at whatever temperature delivers equality under the pressure imposed. Below that temperature, the liquid has the lower chemical potential and any vapour present will condense, whereas above it the vapour has the lower value and the liquid will evaporate. This verbal statement captures every case: transfer proceeds towards the phase with the lower chemical potential and ends at equality.

Phase equilibrium for a pure component at its boiling point rests on one condition, stated in words before any equation is named: the chemical potential of the liquid equals the chemical potential of the vapour. Chemical potential is the quantity whose equality across phases defines equilibrium for a pure substance; while the two values differ, material moves from the phase with the higher value to the phase with the lower one, and the transfer stops when the values meet.

At the boiling point the liquid and the vapour coexist at the same temperature and the same pressure, and neither phase grows at the expense of the other. Heat added at the boiling point does not raise the temperature. The added heat supplies the change of state itself, converting liquid to vapour while the equality of chemical potential is maintained, because a temperature rise would break the equality that the coexistence rests on.

The boiling point is therefore not a property of the liquid alone. A change of pressure moves the temperature at which the two chemical potentials are equal, and boiling occurs at the temperature where the equality holds for the imposed pressure. Below that temperature the liquid has the lower chemical potential and vapour condenses; above it the vapour has the lower value and liquid evaporates. The equilibrium condition in words covers each case without a further rule: transfer runs toward the phase of lower chemical potential and ends at equality.
